scenes.visual: Title: More Progenitors, More Cortical Area. Show the cortical sheet above ventricular and outer progenitor zones.

scenes.tts: Your cortex is only about twice as thick as a mouse's. Yet its surface is roughly a thousand times larger. A leading explanation is more progenitors working for longer. Outer radial glia renew themselves away from the ventricle. Their daughters can become intermediate progenitors, which divide into neurons. This is thought to amplify neuron production. More neurons help build a larger cortical sheet.

scenes.visual: Compare mouse and human cortical sheets schematically, with written labels about twice the thickness and roughly a thousand times the area; do not draw to scale. Immediately reveal the outer subventricular zone. Show an example outer radial glial lineage that renews and produces an intermediate progenitor, then neurons. Link increased output to a larger sheet; label this a leading explanation.

scenes.tts: In living slices of human fetal cortex, researchers filmed these cells dividing. The classic outer radial glial cell keeps a fibre to the brain surface but has no contact with the ventricle. Daughters could divide again or become intermediate progenitors. These cells are abundant in primates and ferret, and rare in mouse. Their fibres fan the scaffold outward, favouring growth in area. The nearly smooth marmoset has them too. They do not guarantee folding.

scenes.visual: Show a human fetal slice, with the ventricle below and outer subventricular zone above. Label the illustrated shape as a classic example. Follow alternative daughter outcomes: renewed radial glia and intermediate progenitors feeding neuron production. Fan the fibres outward. Compare abundance in primates, ferret and mouse, then show the nearly smooth marmoset as a limit on the folding inference.

scenes.tts: Early founders provide another route to more area. Pasko Rakic proposed the radial unit hypothesis from work in the fetal rhesus monkey. In this simplified model, each patch of progenitors makes a column. The number of units sets area. Their neuron output sets thickness. Related neurons can also spread sideways.

scenes.visual: Return to early founders at the ventricle. Label the radial unit diagram simplified model, based on fetal rhesus monkey work. Show patches feeding columns; bracket the row as area and a column height as thickness. Include some lateral dispersal of related neurons.

scenes.tts: While founders divide symmetrically, the pool doubles each round. In the simple model, three extra rounds give eight times as many units. Three extra direct asymmetric divisions add just three neurons per column. In mice, stabilized beta-catenin kept more progenitors cycling. The cortex enlarged and buckled, but this did not reproduce primate cortical growth.

scenes.visual: Show three founder doublings, 1 to 2 to 4 to 8, alongside a column gaining three neurons through extra direct asymmetric divisions. Label the arithmetic conditional on the simplified radial-unit model. Then show stabilized beta-catenin in mouse progenitors, increased cycling and ventricular-surface buckling. Explicitly distinguish this mouse expansion from primate cortical growth.

scenes.tts: Human-specific gene copies act on these processes. A R H G A P eleven B increased basal progenitors in mouse embryos and enlarged the neocortex in marmoset fetuses. Notch two N L kept progenitors dividing in mouse cortex. Deleting it made human organoid progenitors differentiate early. In cultured human fetal slices, blocking A R H G A P eleven B reduced basal progenitors. These tests support contributions to expansion. None shows that one gene made the human cortex.
scenes.narration: Human-specific gene copies act on these processes. ARHGAP11B increased basal progenitors in mouse embryos and enlarged the neocortex in marmoset fetuses. These tests support contributions to expansion. None shows that one gene made the human cortex.

scenes.visual: Use an evidence table with separate rows for ARHGAP11B in mouse embryos, marmoset fetuses and cultured human fetal slices, and NOTCH2NL in mouse cortex and human organoids. Show each stated result beside its system. Label cultured tissue and organoids clearly. Link the rows back to progenitor amplification and continued division; end with contributions, not a single-gene explanation.

scenes.tts: Time matters too. Human cortical neurogenesis lasts longer than in rhesus monkeys or mice. That gives neurogenic progenitors more time to divide. Output also depends on cell-cycle length and division type. Human neurons mature slowly too. Transplanted into newborn mouse cortex, they kept a largely human pace. That is maturation, distinct from producing neurons.

Keep division type and cell-cycle length visible as factors in output. Then depict human neurons transplanted into newborn mouse cortex maturing over a human-like time course. Keep this separate from the progenitor lineage.

scenes.tts: The result broadly fits primate scaling: a human brain holds about the neuron number predicted for a primate brain its size. Mass alone misses where those neurons sit.
